content: The comparison of health goal achievements across various districts is essential for identifying disparities and areas for improvement. Training in data analysis, visualization, and utilization is critical for healthcare providers, facility managers, and personnel involved in data entry, management, and application at the facility level. Patient monitoring data can inform the design of training and capacity-building activities by highlighting both strengths and weaknesses in facility performance. For instance, during training sessions, facilities with low rates of loss to follow-up (LTFU) can share their successful practices and strategies, while facilities with identified service delivery gaps can receive targeted training. For example, facilities with low viral load (VL) suppression rates can benefit from additional on-site support and mentoring focused on managing patients on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with high VL levels. Mentorship from subnational health system levels to facilities can enhance the use of data, including electronic medical record (EMR) reports and tools, to improve clinical management, service delivery, and client tracing. Regular facility data review meetings, held monthly or periodically, can begin with a brief presentation of recent data and trends. These meetings provide opportunities for performance review, information sharing, and reflection on data gaps and weaknesses, encouraging healthcare providers to address these issues. Data staff can present service delivery data and patient alerts during clinical meetings to foster discussions on strengths, weaknesses, potential interventions for poor outcomes, missing or incomplete data, data backlogs, and mentoring needs. Patient monitoring tools should generate actionable reports that clearly define responsibilities at each sublevel, ensuring data availability at the appropriate level and clarifying roles for follow-up actions. Analyzing LTFU data is crucial for supporting client tracing efforts. Patients reported as LTFU often include unidentified deaths, unrecorded transfers, and individuals genuinely lost to follow-up. This analysis helps determine treatment outcomes and supports re-engagement in care. Routine analysis of LTFU data should be conducted to understand patient losses and facilitate re-engagement. Records should be updated with this information to improve service delivery, adherence, retention, and program reporting. Data can also trigger patient recall through telephone follow-ups and home visits. For example, periodic reviews of patients who missed appointments by more than seven days or lack antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for over seven days can identify individuals for recall and tracing interventions. Facilities should review these data to identify actions that could improve patient engagement and experience. Addressing LTFU is particularly important in the context of scaling up differentiated service delivery (DSD) models, such as multi-month dispensing, where tracking patient follow-up is critical. Routine and timely data reviews at site, district, and national levels can provide insights into transfer-in and transfer-out issues and explain data quality challenges. In Cape Town, South Africa, subdistrict meetings are held quarterly to review aggregated patient monitoring data and use the findings to enhance service delivery. Challenges and successes in individual clinic performance are highlighted, and potential reasons are addressed through experience sharing and recommendations. For example, using aggregate patient monitoring data, a district identified challenges in early HIV VL testing completion rates (3–6 months after ART initiation) across facilities. Data review revealed that Clinic C had below-average performance for two consecutive quarters. Addressing these performance issues required reviewing individual patient records using a line list of patients. Clinic C investigated the reasons for low early VL testing coverage by holding management meetings with clinical, clerical, and patient-support staff. The investigation involved determining whether the issue was related to data or clinical/patient management. Steps included extracting a line list of ART-initiated patients, retrieving VL test dates and results, comparing ART initiation dates with VL test results, and analyzing the data after excluding deaths, losses to care, and transfers out. Findings revealed both data errors and missed VL testing opportunities by clinicians due to time constraints and high patient loads. To improve early VL testing coverage, the head clinician recommended ongoing in-house training, proper use of patient monitoring tools, regular audits, and avoiding postponing blood sample collection. Clerical staff were tasked with organizing patient folders daily, printing test results for patient visits, and capturing and filing test results, including VL data. Counselors were instructed to systematically check patient folders and refer patients for VL testing at appropriate times. The guidance also outlines steps for adapting and implementing an HIV patient monitoring system, emphasizing the importance of meeting minimum requirements for quality patient care. These steps include forming a technical working group, engaging stakeholders, inventorying current tools, defining indicators and datasets, and reviewing the digital health ecosystem. Adapting tools based on national guidelines, developing training materials, and ensuring systematic follow-up after training are also critical. Human resources and capacity-building are essential for effective patient monitoring. Task-shifting to lower-level cadres and lay providers can enhance program efficiency. Collaboration with external institutions and stakeholders can facilitate access to resources and improve patient care and program monitoring. In summary, a robust HIV patient monitoring system requires standardized tools, clear roles and responsibilities, regular data reviews, and targeted interventions to address gaps. Effective use of data can improve service delivery, patient outcomes, and program performance.
